056.subtitle: The great tantra, the great mantra, the great diagram

commentary.meaning: Six names, and every one of them opens with mahā-. The verse sits near the end of a long chain of great-names that has been running since the fifty-third verse, and it is the point at which that chain stops describing her attributes and starts naming the apparatus of her worship. Three of the six are the three instruments a tantric tradition works with — the system of doctrine and practice, the formula that is spoken, the diagram that is drawn — and each of the three is claimed as her possession rather than as the practitioner's equipment. Then comes the seat she occupies, then the rite by which she is approached, and only at the end the worshipper. The order is deliberate: doctrine, sound, form, throne, liturgy, devotee. And the devotee the verse finally names is not a human being. It is Bhairava, Śiva in the form that terrifies, setting his terror down in order to perform the worship himself.
commentary.history:
Take the three technical words apart before doing anything else with them, because all three are perfectly ordinary Sanskrit nouns built on perfectly ordinary roots, and a learner who meets them first as an exotic triad will never see that. Tantra comes from √tan, to stretch: the warp stretched on a loom, and from there any framework, system or arrangement, and finally a class of revealed text and the practice it prescribes. Mantra comes from √man, to think, with the suffix -tra that forms instrument nouns: a device for thinking with. Yantra comes from √yam, to hold or restrain, with the same suffix: a device for holding something in place. Yantra is the everyday word for a machine, for a water-lifting engine, for the mechanism of a lock. So the triad is not three mysteries but three tools, distinguished by what each of them holds: the system holds the teaching, the formula holds the sound, the diagram holds the form.

For this school the three have particular referents. The tantra is the Śrīvidyā corpus, the mantra is the fifteen-syllabled pañcadaśākṣarī whose three segments the nyāsa before the stotra has already placed on the reciter's body, and the yantra is the Śrīcakra, the nine interlocking triangles with their surrounding lotuses and enclosures. What the verse adds to all three is possession. The compounds are bahuvrīhis: she whose tantra is the great one, she whose mantra is the great one, she whose yantra is the great one. The practitioner who thinks of the mantra as something he has acquired is being corrected in the space of three names.

The Saundaryalaharī makes the same point with a story. Śiva, it says, put sixty-four tantras into the world, each of them able to produce one particular power and nothing else, and then stopped; it took her insistence to bring down the one system that could deliver everything a human life is for. Lists of those sixty-four exist and disagree with one another, and the disagreement is itself informative: what the number is doing is marking a completed set, not counting titles on a shelf. Against a complete but fragmentary sixty-four, mahātantrā names the one that is whole.

Mahāsanā, she whose seat is great, admits two readings and the tradition uses both. Five verses further on, the stotra will seat her on a couch made of five corpses who are the five great gods, and mahāsanā is the compressed anticipation of that. It is also read of the central point of the Śrīcakra, the bindu, where she is invoked and where the whole diagram converges. Neither reading is figurative in the way a modern reader might expect: in the rite, an ordinary metal or crystal plate is treated as the actual furniture of an actual throne room, and everything offered is offered to somebody sitting there.

The fifth name is the one to slow down over, because it turns on the word krama, sequence. Mahāyāgakramārādhyā does not say she is worshipped by the great rite; it says she is worshipped by the order of the great rite. Śrīcakra worship proceeds through nine enclosures, each with its own resident goddesses, and the practitioner may travel them outward from the centre, in the order of emission, or inward from the outermost square, in the order of reabsorption, or hold to the middle order of maintenance. Which direction is taken changes what the rite means. To insert krama into the name is to say that the sequence is not an administrative detail of the liturgy but part of what is being offered.

Bhairava, in the last name, is the form of Śiva that carries a skull and haunts the cremation ground, and the Sanskrit tradition connects the word with bhīru and bhaya, fear. A large body of tantric scripture is named after him — the Bhairava tantras — and in the Kashmirian schools Bhairava is not a fierce aspect of the absolute but simply a name of the absolute, unpacked as the one who supports, holds and dissolves the universe. Either way the name closes the verse with a reversal that the stotra likes and will use again: the most frightening thing anyone can imagine is here found in the posture of a worshipper, with his hands full of flowers.
commentary.practice:
The first line is four names of four syllables each, laid down like four beats of a drum, and it is the most mechanically dangerous line in this part of the stotra. Mahātantrā, mahāmantrā, mahāyantrā differ from one another by a single consonant. Reciters lose their place here, repeat a name, or drop one, and the loss is almost impossible to hear. The remedy is to fix the order by its logic rather than by its sound: system, then formula, then figure — the thing thought, the thing said, the thing drawn. Once you know why they come in that order you will not transpose them.

The cluster in all three is ntr, three consonants in a row: dental n, dental t, and r. English has nothing like it and will want to swallow the t. Say tan-tra with the n fully closed at the teeth, the t released, and the r following as its own articulation. Then hold the tongue exactly where it is and change only the opening consonant to get man-tra and yan-tra. Doing the three in sequence at half speed is a better drill for the dental series than any isolated word.

Every name in this verse carries mahā with a long second vowel, and the metre depends on it. Six long ās in the first line alone, and the temptation under speed is to clip them to something like the a of mahā's first syllable. Keep the two vowels of mahā distinctly unequal in length and the anuṣṭubh holds its shape by itself.

In the second line, mahāyāgakramārādhyā hides a join worth seeing. The elements are mahāyāga, krama and ārādhyā; krama ends in short a, ārādhyā begins in long ā, and a short a followed by a long ā gives a single long ā. So kramārādhyā is krama plus ārādhyā, and the word ārādhyā — to be propitiated, a gerundive from ā-√rādh — is the same formation you have already met in ārādhitā elsewhere in the hymn. The cluster dhy in ārādhyā is an aspirated dental followed by the palatal glide: d, breath, y, with no gap.

Mahābhairavapūjitā gives you the diphthong ai in bhairava, which is a full-length vowel, not the short glide of English "eye", and a long ū in pūjitā. The bh at the head of bhairava is a single aspirated labial, not b followed by h.

The caesura falls where it always does in an anuṣṭubh, after the sixteenth syllable, which here is the end of mahāsanā — a clean break between the four short names and the two long ones. Breathe there and nowhere else.

For the recitation done as archanā, these names are turned into the dative: mahātantrāyai namaḥ, mahāmantrāyai namaḥ, and so on. Every one of the six is a feminine ā-stem, so every one takes -āyai, and this verse is therefore about as good a place as exists in the stotra to fix that ending in the ear by repetition. As for what to hold while chanting it: you are using a formula, following a sequence, and sitting in front of a diagram, and the verse is telling you that all three belong to somebody else.

057.subtitle: Witness of the dance at the end of the world

commentary.meaning: Three names, and the first one takes an entire line to itself. It puts her at the end of everything: the worlds are being withdrawn, Śiva is dancing the dance that withdraws them, and she is the one who sees it happen. The second name gives her a title from the court rather than the cremation ground — not consort or beloved but mahiṣī, the consecrated chief queen, a constitutional position with rites of its own. The third simply names her, and it is the name under which this whole tradition knows her: Mahātripurasundarī, the great beauty of the three cities. Read together the three move from the outer limit of time inward to a throne and then to a proper name, and the pivot of the whole verse is the word sākṣiṇī. She is not described as surviving the dissolution or as causing it. She is described as watching it, which in the philosophical vocabulary this stotra draws on is a far stronger claim than either.
commentary.history:
Sākṣin is the word that carries this verse, and it is worth taking apart. It is built from sa, with, and akṣi, the eye: one who was there with his own eyes. In ordinary Sanskrit it is the legal term for a witness in a lawsuit. Vedānta borrowed it and made it technical, and in that use the sākṣin is consciousness considered purely as that before which things appear — never an agent, never affected by what it registers, present equally in waking and dream and dreamless sleep. The point of calling her the witness of the tāṇḍava is therefore not that she is brave enough to watch. It is that the final destruction of the universe is an event, and events happen in front of awareness, and awareness is not one of the things that can be destroyed. The stotra will develop exactly this in five verses' time, when it runs her through waking, dream and sleep and then calls her the fourth.

The dance itself has a technical name. Tāṇḍava is the vigorous, masculine style, set against lāsya, the gentle and lyrical one; the Nāṭyaśāstra makes Taṇḍu, an attendant of Śiva, the teacher of it, and the tradition has always heard the attendant's name inside the word. When it is performed at the close of a kalpa it is the destruction itself and not a representation of it — the same idea that the bronze Naṭarāja figures of the Cōḻa period state in metal, with the drum of emission in one hand and the fire of withdrawal in the other. A kalpa is a day of Brahmā, at the end of which the worlds are drawn in; the purāṇas give figures for its length and do not entirely agree, and the compound here is best heard as naming the great dissolution rather than a unit on a calendar.

Mahiṣī is not a poetic word for wife. In the Vedic royal consecration the king has several wives with distinct ritual standing, and the mahiṣī is the first of them, the one anointed alongside him and the one with a part to play in the horse sacrifice. The literal sense of the noun is unglamorous — mahiṣa is a buffalo, mahiṣī the female of it — and what it conveys is bulk, weight, standing. So the name places her beside Kāmeśvara as a matter of constitutional fact, not of affection. That she is queen specifically of Kāmeśa, the lord of desire, keeps the tradition's central claim in view: the power at the top of this system is not renunciant.

The third name is the school's own. Tripurasundarī is the deity of the fifteen-syllabled mantra, and mahā- here does not add a superlative so much as mark the full form of the title. The three cities have been read in as many ways as there are commentators, and the readings are worth knowing because they are not alternatives so much as layers: the three cities burnt by Śiva in the old myth; the three states of waking, dream and sleep; the three bodies, gross, subtle and causal; the three segments of her mantra; the three sets of lines that structure the Śrīcakra; the three powers of will, knowledge and action. What all the readings share is that she is not in one of the three but presides over the set.

One last thing about the shape of this verse. The stotra has been piling up mahā- names for five verses, and here the prefix does something different in each of the three. In the first name it is distributed — a great lord, a great dissolution, a great dance — so that mahā occurs three times inside one word. In the second it modifies the husband. In the third it modifies the title itself. The chain is not running on inertia; it is being worked.
commentary.practice:
The first line is a single word sixteen syllables long, which makes it one of the longest names in the hymn and the one most likely to be taken at a run. Do not run it. It has an internal structure you can lean on: maheśvara, mahākalpa, mahātāṇḍava, sākṣiṇī — four pieces, the first three of which each begin with mahā. Say it as four, with no breath between them but with the seams audible.

Two places in this verse show the same sandhi and it is one of the most common in the language. Mahā ends in ā; īśvara begins in ī; a followed by i, in either length, gives e. So maheśvara is mahā plus īśvara, and in the second line mahākāmeśa is mahākāma plus īśa. Once you can hear e as the fused product of a and i you will start finding it everywhere in this text, and it will stop being an arbitrary vowel.

Tāṇḍava gives the retroflex pair ṇḍ: the tongue-tip curls back for the nasal and stays curled for the stop, with no forward movement between them. This is the same cluster as in kuṇḍa in the fourth name of the stotra and in maṇḍala later on, and it is worth drilling as a unit rather than as two sounds.

Sākṣiṇī packs a great deal into four syllables. The kṣ is a conjunct of k and the retroflex ṣ, and Sanskrit treats it as a single cluster; the ṇ that follows is retroflex too, so the tongue-tip is back for the ṣ, forward and up for nothing at all, and back again for the ṇ. Say sāk-ṣi-ṇī slowly. Then contrast it with mahiṣī in the next line, where the ṣ is retroflex but the vowel around it is short and the ending is a long ī. Sākṣiṇī and mahiṣī are a good minimal drill for the retroflex sibilant in two different environments.

Sundarī is easier than it looks and is often mispronounced anyway. The n is dental — tongue-tip against the back of the upper teeth — and the d that follows is dental too. Nothing in this word is retroflex, which is precisely why it is worth saying immediately after tāṇḍava and sākṣiṇī, so the ear registers the difference.

The caesura is after the sixteenth syllable, which here is the end of the first line and therefore the end of the first name. That is unusual and it means this verse breathes in two halves rather than four quarters. Give the whole of the first line one arc.

What to hold while chanting it: the temptation is to picture the dance, because the dance is spectacular. Resist it and stay with the watcher. The verse spends fourteen of its sixteen opening syllables setting up a catastrophe and then, in the last two, tells you that somebody is looking at it calmly. That is the content. In practice the second and third names are often used on their own — mahātripurasundarī is the standard invocation of this tradition and appears at the head of countless ritual manuals — but taken out of the verse they lose the reason the title is being conferred.

commentary.meaning: One number, said three times. The verse gives her sixty-four acts of ritual attendance, then declares her to be made of the sixty-four arts, then surrounds her with yoginīs reckoned in sixty-four crores. The three names move outward in a way that is easy to miss: the first is what a worshipper does to her, the second is what she consists of, the third is who else is in the room. Between them they take a number that in Indian culture simply means a complete set and use it to describe a rite, a curriculum and a retinue. The middle name is the interesting one. To say that she is made of the sixty-four arts is to say that singing, painting, carpentry, cookery, gem-testing and the training of parrots are not activities performed in her presence but material she is composed of, which is a considerably stronger claim about the world than the surrounding verses have been making.
commentary.history:
Sixty-four is four cubed, and it recurs across Indian learning wherever a set needs to be marked as complete: sixty-four tantras, sixty-four yoginīs, sixty-four bhairavas, sixty-four arts, and here sixty-four ritual services. It is not a count arrived at by counting. It is a shape the mind can hold, in the same way that a hundred and eight is, and lists that carry the number regularly turn out to contain a different number of items when you actually enumerate them.

The upacāras are the most concrete thing in the verse, and the least often explained. Upacāra means an approach or an attendance — literally a going-near — and the underlying idea is domestic hospitality: what you do for an honoured guest who has come to your house. Ordinary image-worship uses sixteen of them, the ṣoḍaśopacāra, and most temple ritual anywhere in India is a variant of that list. The elaborate Śrīvidyā rite uses sixty-four, and they are worth reading in order at least once, because they are not sixty-four kinds of incense. They are a morning. The old ornaments are taken off; there is a massage with scented oil; she is led into the bathing hall and seated on a jewelled stool; hot water; drying; red silk and a red upper cloth; then into the anointing hall for sandal, aloe, saffron, musk, camphor; incense held under the mass of her hair; garlands of jasmine, campaka, aśoka; then into the jewel hall for the crown of nine gems, the crescent, vermilion in the parting of the hair, collyrium, earrings, a nose ornament, lac for the lower lip; then necklaces, armlets by the pair, bangles, rings, girdle, anklets; then the noose in one hand, the goad in another, the sugarcane bow in the third, the flower arrows in the fourth; then she mounts the great cakra and takes her seat on Kāmeśvara's lap; then a cup of nectar, water for the mouth, camphored betel, laughter; then the waving of lamps, the parasol, two fly-whisks, a mirror, a fan. The list ends with scent, flower, incense, lamp and food — which is to say that the sixty-four services finish at the point where an ordinary short worship begins.

Kalā in the second name is one of the great multipurpose words of Sanskrit and this is the verse to learn it in. Its root sense is a small division of something larger. From that it means a sixteenth part; a digit of the moon; a fraction of time; and, in the sense used here, a skill or an art, a discrete competence that can be enumerated and taught. All the meanings stay alive at once, so catuḥṣaṣṭikalāmayī can be heard as made of the sixty-four arts and equally as made of sixty-four parts. The word will matter again: this recension divides the thousand names into kalās, and the moon and the sun are each said to have their own set of them.

The standard list of the sixty-four arts is Vātsyāyana's, in the third chapter of the first book of the Kāmasūtra, where they are prescribed as the education of a cultivated person alongside the Kāmasūtra itself. Other lists exist and differ; his is simply the best known. What is striking about it is how unhierarchical it is. Singing, instrumental music, dance and painting come first, but the same list contains the cutting of stencils for face-decoration, arrangements of coloured rice and flowers, the making of flower-beds, tooth powders and body paints, water-games, garland design, perfumery, conjuring, sleight of hand, cookery, the mixing of drinks, needlework, riddles, recitation, carpentry, architecture, the testing of gems, metallurgy, arboriculture, the arranging of cock and quail fights, teaching parrots and mynas to talk, massage, codes and secret writing, knowledge of regional languages, prosody, lexicography, and physical training. A goddess who is made of that list is being credited with skill as such, from the highest art to the most domestic knack.

The last name is the loudest and the least literal. A koṭi is ten million, so sixty-four koṭis is six hundred and forty million yoginīs, and no one is being asked to audit the figure. But the sixty-four yoginīs behind the hyperbole were the object of a real and geographically specific cult, and it left buildings. Circular open-air temples survive at Hirapur and Ranipur-Jharial in Odisha, at Bheraghat near Jabalpur, and at Mitaoli in the Morena district, most of them built between the ninth and the twelfth centuries. They are round, roofless, and lined on the inside with niches, each niche holding one goddess facing the centre. The lists of names differ from site to site, and the number is sometimes eighty-one instead of sixty-four. When this verse says she is served by troops of yoginīs it is not inventing a decorative crowd; it is invoking a form of worship that people once walked into.
commentary.practice:
This verse is the hardest thing to say in the whole of this stretch of the stotra, and the difficulty is concentrated in one word. Catuḥṣaṣṭi is catur, four, plus ṣaṣṭi, sixty — Sanskrit counts four-and-sixty, like the older English. The r of catur has become a visarga before the sibilant, and ṣaṣṭi itself has a retroflex sibilant followed by a retroflex stop. So in five syllables you have a visarga, then ṣ, then ṣṭ. The tongue-tip curls back and stays back. Say ca-tuḥ-ṣaṣ-ṭi at half speed until the two ṣ sounds are identical to each other and neither of them has drifted forward into an English "sh".

Then the compound makes it worse. In catuḥṣaṣṭyupacārāḍhyā, the final i of ṣaṣṭi meets the u of upacāra and becomes the glide y, which is the sandhi rule that turns i into y before any dissimilar vowel. That leaves the cluster ṣṭy: retroflex sibilant, retroflex stop, palatal glide, three articulations with the tongue moving back, staying back, then springing forward. And the word ends in āḍhyā, which is an aspirated retroflex ḍh followed by y. Two of the nastiest clusters in the language are in one word, and there is no way round them except slowly.

Against that, the second half of the first line is a rest. Catuḥṣaṣṭikalāmayī has no conjunct after the opening, and the suffix -mayī, feminine of -maya, means simply made of — the same suffix as in cinmayī three verses later. Let the line relax there.

The second line is one name of sixteen syllables: mahācatuḥṣaṣṭikoṭiyoginīgaṇasevitā. The caesura falls after the eighth syllable, which lands inside the word between koṭi and yoginī. Hear the pause without opening a gap in the sound, the same discipline the fourth meditation verse asks for. Yoginī has a plain dental n and gaṇa has a retroflex ṇ, and they are three syllables apart, so this is another of the free drills the stotra keeps handing out.

One small grammatical point that helps the sense. Āḍhya means rich in, well supplied with, and it governs an instrumental: rich by means of the sixty-four services. Mayī means consisting of. Sevitā is a past passive participle, waited upon. So the three names are grammatically three different relations — she is enriched by the first sixty-four, composed of the second, attended by the third — and knowing that keeps the verse from sounding like a chant on a single number.

In archanā the names become catuḥṣaṣṭyupacārāḍhyāyai namaḥ and so on, which is a mouthful worth attempting precisely because it forces the ṣṭy cluster to be produced twice in one breath. If you can manage that dative you have solved the verse.

What to hold while chanting: the number is a claim about scope, not about quantity. Sixty-four means all of them.

commentary.meaning: Two lines built to exactly the same measure — four syllables, four syllables, eight — and each of them bound together by a word repeated three times. In the first line the word is candra, the moon, and it does three different jobs: it is the name of a teacher who handed down her formula, then the name of the same teacher again by implication, then the actual lunar disc at whose centre she is said to abide. In the second line the word is cāru, lovely, and it simply repeats, giving her a lovely form, a lovely smile, and a lovely crescent to wear. So the verse begins in the driest possible territory — the transmission history of a mantra, teacher by teacher — and ends by describing a woman's face and her jewellery. The hinge between the two is the third name, where the teacher's name turns into the moon itself, and the moon then supplies the last word of the verse.
commentary.history:
Vidyā is a technical term here and not the general word for knowledge, so start with that. It comes from √vid, to know, and it is grammatically feminine. In tantric usage that grammatical fact was put to work: the mantra of a goddess is called her vidyā, while the mantra of a male deity is a mantra. The fifteen-syllabled formula of this school is therefore the Śrīvidyā, and the school takes its name from the formula. When the stotra says manuvidyā it is not saying that she knows what Manu knew. It is saying that she is the formula in the form Manu handed it on — that the goddess and the syllables are the same object seen twice.

Behind the two names lies the tradition's account of how the vidyā came down. It speaks of a set of teachers, each associated with his own recension, and the number usually given is twelve; the lists differ by a name or two depending on which handbook you consult, which is worth knowing before treating any single list as authoritative. Manu and Candra stand at the head of most versions of it, and Kubera, Lopāmudrā, Manmatha, Agastya, Sūrya, Indra, Skanda, Śiva and Durvāsas appear in most. Only a few of these recensions survive as living practice; the two most widely followed are named after the syllable each begins with — the kādi line traced to Manmatha and the hādi line traced to Lopāmudrā. What the stotra does with all of this is quietly radical. It names two of the teachers and then declines to make her their pupil or their possession. She is the vidyā, in Manu's version and in Candra's alike, which means that a difference of lineage is a difference in how she is spoken and not a difference in who she is.

Then candra stops being a teacher and becomes the moon. This stotra has already put the moon on her forehead, made her face into a moon, and hung the eighth-night half-disc above her brow; now it places her at the centre of the lunar orb. The tradition counts sixteen digits in the moon, and worships them by name in the ritual preparation of the vessels: the same handbook that gives the twelve digits of the sun gives amṛtā, mānadā, pūṣā, tuṣṭi, puṣṭi, rati, dhṛti, śaśinī, candrikā, kānti, jyotsnā, śrī, prīti, aṅgadā, pūrṇā and pūrṇāmṛtā. Fifteen of the sixteen are what the eye sees waxing and waning across a fortnight. The sixteenth never appears and never diminishes, and the tradition connects that hidden digit with the hidden syllable that turns the fifteen-syllabled vidyā into the sixteen-syllabled one. To be at the centre of the disc is to be the part of it that does not change.

Cāru is a much simpler word and a very old one: pleasing, agreeable, esteemed, beautiful. The dictionary's range runs from beloved to merely pretty, and the stotra uses it three times in a row without embarrassment. There is a real change of register here after the lineage names, and it is not a lapse. A hymn that has just told you the goddess is a transmitted formula immediately tells you she has a nice smile, and the juxtaposition is the theology: the object of this practice is not an abstraction that happens to have been given a face.

The crescent in the last name has a history of its own. Śiva wears a digit of the moon in his matted hair, and the purāṇas explain it variously — as the digit spared when Dakṣa's curse consumed the rest, as his share of the churning of the ocean. On him it is a trophy of an old crisis. Here she simply wears one, and the poet's adjective is cāru: it is lovely. The stotra has been consistent about this. Everything that on Śiva is the residue of some ordeal is on her an ornament chosen because it suits her.
commentary.practice:
The most useful thing you can notice about this verse is its symmetry, because once you have it the verse recites itself. Both lines are four syllables, then four, then eight. Manuvidyā, candravidyā, candramaṇḍalamadhyagā. Cārurūpā, cāruhāsā, cārucandrakalādharā. The two short names in each line begin with the same element, and the long name in each line begins with it too. Nothing else in this part of the stotra is built so tightly, and hearing the two lines as answering each other is most of the work.

The first vowel is where the accuracy lies. Cāru has a long ā in its first syllable; candra has a short a. They are adjacent in the second line — cārucandra — and the contrast between the two is the whole rhythm of that word. Say cā for two beats and can for one, and the eight-syllable name falls into place.

Candra also gives you the cluster ndr: a dental n, a dental d and an r, three separate articulations with no vowel between them. Do not let the d disappear. Practise it against candrikā and candana, both of which you will meet elsewhere in this hymn.

Maṇḍala has the retroflex pair ṇḍ — tongue-tip curled back for both — immediately followed by a dental l, which is the sharpest back-to-front movement in the verse. Then madhyagā gives you dhy, an aspirated dental with the palatal glide after it: d, breath, y, said as one release rather than as three.

Vidyā has the conjunct dy, dental d into palatal y. It occurs twice in the first line and it is the single most useful cluster to get right in this verse, because the word will recur throughout the stotra and throughout the tradition.

The palatal c of cāru is an affricate made with the tongue-body flat against the hard palate, the same place as the y of yes. English speakers tend to produce the sound of "church", which is close enough to be understood and slightly too far forward. Aim it back.

One sandhi worth seeing: cārucandrakalādharā ends in -dharā, from √dhṛ, to hold or wear, and the a of kalā fuses with the a of dhara in the ordinary way. Dharā is an agent form, not a participle, so the name says she is a wearer of the crescent rather than that a crescent has been placed on her. The difference is small and it is the difference between an ornament and a burden.

What to hold while chanting it: the verse hands you a transmission and then a face. If you are using it as a contemplation on its own, the place to rest is the third name — not the moon in the sky but the middle of it, the part that neither waxes nor wanes and that nobody has ever seen.

060.subtitle: The king of diagrams, and the mountain's daughter

commentary.meaning: The verse turns on a change of consonant. Its first line is two eight-syllable names both beginning in c, and both of them are about jurisdiction: she rules everything that moves and everything that does not, and she lives in the diagram that outranks every other diagram. Then the second line switches to p and switches scale with it. Pārvatī — a personal name, taken from her father's mountain. Lotus eyes. A complexion like a ruby. In the space of one line the sovereign of the moving and the unmoving world becomes a particular young woman with a particular face, born in a particular range of hills. Nothing in the verse marks the transition or apologises for it, and that is the point: the two halves are not two aspects to be reconciled but one subject described twice, once from very far away and once from close enough to see her eyes.
commentary.history:
Carācara is worth a moment because it is a habit of thought as much as a word. Cara is what moves; a-cara is what does not; put together they mean everything there is. Sanskrit prefers to say totality by naming a pair of opposites rather than by using a word for all, and the same manoeuvre gives sthāvara-jaṅgama, standing and going, and dyāvāpṛthivī, heaven and earth. There is an extra turn in this case. Jagat, the ordinary word for world, is itself a present participle of √gam, to go — the world is literally the thing that is going. So a compound that includes acara inside a phrase about the jagat is quietly saying that the going thing contains what does not go, and that both are under one rule.

Cakrarāja is the Śrīcakra, and niketana means a dwelling — a house, a residence, the place someone actually lives. She is not depicted in the diagram and not symbolised by it; she is at home in it. The construction is described in the Saundaryalaharī more precisely than anywhere else in the devotional literature: four triangles with their apex upward, taken as Śiva, and five with their apex downward, taken as Śakti, overlaid so that their intersections generate a field of smaller triangles, and around that the eight-petalled lotus, the sixteen-petalled lotus, three circles and a triple-lined square with four gates — nine enclosures in all. That verse also gives an interesting textual problem. It says forty-four, and the count of small triangles in the drawing as it is normally executed is forty-three. Manuscripts of the poem preserve both readings, forty-four and forty-three, and commentators who keep forty-four generally reach it by counting the central point as one more. It is a good example of how a tradition handles arithmetic that will not quite close: it does not suppress the discrepancy, it records the variant.

Then the tone changes. The stotra has used proper names before — Bhavānī, Durgā, Mahālakṣmī all stand earlier in the thousand — but Pārvatī is the first that identifies her by parentage. It is a vṛddhi derivative, the type of formation that lengthens the first vowel of a stem to mean belonging to or descended from: parvata, a mountain, gives pārvatī, the mountain's daughter. Kālidāsa builds the opening of the Kumārasambhava out of exactly this etymology, first spending twelve verses on the Himālaya as a person and only then producing the daughter whose name is simply his. The name is thus the opposite of every name in the first line: not a title conferred by function but the ordinary patronymic that any child of that household would carry.

The two lotus names close the verse and they pun on each other. Padma is the lotus; padmarāga, lotus-coloured, is the ruby. So the same word gives her eyes and her complexion, once as a flower and once as a stone. The stotra has been reaching for red gems since its first verses and has already used three different words for a ruby; padmarāga has appeared before, of her cheeks. What is new here is samaprabhā, equal in radiance, which for once does not defeat the thing compared. After a long run of names in which coral and the bimba fruit and a mirror of ruby were all put to shame, this one simply says she shines as much as a ruby does. It is a rest.

One small point about placement. This verse sits at the exact centre of the fourth of the divisions this recension marks in the thousand names, and it does the same thing in miniature that the whole hymn does: it starts at the outside of the diagram and moves in until there is a face.
commentary.practice:
Say this verse immediately after the previous two and the first thing you will notice is relief. There is not a single retroflex consonant in it — no ṭ, no ḍ, no ṇ, no ṣ anywhere in either line. Every stop and nasal is dental, labial, palatal or guttural. After the ṣṭy of catuḥṣaṣṭyupacārāḍhyā and the ṇḍ of candramaṇḍala, the tongue-tip gets to stay forward for thirty-two syllables. Use the verse as a chance to hear what your dental n and d actually sound like when nothing retroflex is pulling at them.

The alliteration does the structural work. Two names in c, then three in p. Line one is eight plus eight; line two is three plus five plus eight. Knowing that pārvatī is only three syllables stops you from stretching it, which is the commonest fault here — reciters give the name more weight than the metre allows because they recognise it.

Carācara contains a sandhi that carries the meaning. The word is cara plus acara, and a short a followed by a short a gives a single long ā. So the long vowel in the middle of the word is the seam where moving meets unmoving. Reciters who shorten it are not just mispronouncing; they are erasing the negative particle and leaving the word saying nothing.

Jagannāthā shows the other common junction. Jagat ends in t; nātha begins in n; a final t before a nasal becomes the corresponding nasal, giving jagan-nātha with a doubled n. Hold both n's. This is the same rule that gives cinmayī in the next verse, where cit plus maya becomes cinmaya, and seeing them a verse apart fixes it.

The cluster kr in cakrarāja is straightforward but often rushed; give the k its own release before the r. Padma has dm, a dental into a labial, which most English speakers manage without trouble. Pārvatī has rv, and the r in Sanskrit is a tap or a light trill, not the American approximant — a single flick of the tongue-tip.

The long vowels are the skeleton of the line: carācara, jagannāthā, cakrarāja, pārvatī, padmarāga, samaprabhā. Every name still ends in the long ā of the feminine nominative singular, as almost all thousand do, except pārvatī, which ends in the long ī of its own stem class. In archanā that difference surfaces at once: the ā-stems take -āyai, so carācarajagannāthāyai namaḥ, but pārvatī is an ī-stem and takes -yai, giving pārvatyai namaḥ. This verse is therefore a free lesson in the two commonest feminine datives in the whole nāmāvalī.

What to hold while chanting: resist the urge to treat the second line as a softening of the first. A diagram of nine enclosures and a girl from the hills are being asserted as the same person, without a joint, and the verse gives you exactly one breath at the caesura to accept it.

commentary.meaning: The two halves of this verse look as though they belong to different books. The first line seats her on a piece of furniture made out of dead gods and then identifies the same five gods as forms of her. The second line abandons imagery entirely and gives three names in the flat vocabulary of the Upaniṣads: made of consciousness, filled with the highest bliss, a solid mass of knowing. The verse works only if you take the halves as one sentence. The five great powers of the universe lie inert beneath her because whatever animation they have is hers and not their own; and what she has that they lack is not more strength but awareness. Read that way, the second line is the reason for the first, and the couch is not a boast about rank. It is a diagram of what happens to anything, including a god, when consciousness is subtracted from it.
commentary.history:
The five are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara and Sadāśiva, and they are the standard five of Śaiva theology, associated with the five cosmic acts that this stotra will list three verses further on. In the visualisation the four lesser ones are the legs of the couch and Sadāśiva is the board laid across them, and she sits on the board. The word for what they are is deliberately brutal. A preta is a corpse, or the wandering shade of one; the participle means gone forth, departed, from pra-√i. There is nothing gentle about the picture and it is not meant to be gentle. It is meant to be a proof.

The reasoning behind it is the same as the reasoning in the Saundaryalaharī's opening verse, which the tradition quotes whenever this question comes up: joined with Śakti, Śiva can bring things about; without her, the god cannot so much as stir. Corpses on a couch are that sentence turned into furniture. Tantric teachers put the point more bluntly still with a play on words that has become proverbial — śiva without śakti is śava, a body. It is a pun rather than an argument, but it is an accurate summary of the doctrine, and the fifth verse of this same poem describes a dissolution in which Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Yama, Kubera and the ranks of Indra are all dead or unconscious while Śiva alone continues to move.

Pañcabrahmasvarūpiṇī then says the same thing from the other side. In Śaiva usage the five brahmans are the five faces of Sadāśiva — Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna — and they correspond, face by face, to the five acts of creating, preserving, withdrawing, veiling and blessing. So the pair of names in the first line is not repetition. In the first she is above them; in the second she is them. The transition between those two claims — from mistress of the five to identity with the five — is the argument the whole verse is making, and it is exactly the transition the second line goes on to justify.

Cinmayī is built with the suffix -maya, which means made of, consisting of, and which the grammarians allow both for material and for essence. Cit is consciousness in the bare sense of awareness, not thought and not mind; the stotra used the same word in its fourth name, where she rose out of a fire-pit made of cit. This is the second time in the thousand names that the poem has reached for the plainest possible term for awareness, and both times it has done so at a moment when it wanted to say what she is rather than what she is like.

Vijñānaghanarūpiṇī is a direct quotation from the Upaniṣads in all but the prefix. The word there is generally prajñānaghana or vijñānaghana — the manuscripts vary and the sense does not — and the image is developed at length in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, where a lump of rock salt is used to explain it: cut it anywhere and it is salt; it has no interior that is not salt, no inside and no outside. Ghana is exactly that, a solid lump, a compacted mass, the same word used of a cloud and of a hammer. So the name is not saying she has a great deal of knowledge. It is saying there is no cross-section of her at which awareness would fail to be present, which is a statement about density rather than quantity.

Paramānandā, standing between the two, is the third term of the formula that Vedānta abbreviates as sat-cit-ānanda, being, awareness and bliss. The Taittirīya's treatment of ānanda is the one the tradition has in mind: not pleasure, which has a cause and therefore an end, but the state of a being who has nothing left to fear. Placed where it is, between consciousness and the mass of knowing, it keeps the line from becoming purely epistemological. Whatever this awareness is, it is not neutral about being itself.
commentary.practice:
Both lines of this verse are dominated by the nasal that most learners never quite believe in. Pañca has ñ, the palatal nasal, made with the tongue-body against the hard palate — the same place as the c that follows it, which is why the two sit together. It is not the n of "pan" and not the ny of "canyon" said quickly. Set the tongue for c, then let air out through the nose, then release into the c. Pañca opens both names in the first line, so you get two chances at it in eight syllables.

Pañcapretāsanāsīnā contains two vowel fusions in a row and they are worth unpicking, because the word looks impenetrable and is not. The pieces are pañca, preta, āsana and āsīna. Preta ends in a short a and āsana begins with a long ā: short a plus long ā gives a single long ā. Āsana ends in a short a and āsīna begins with a long ā: the same rule again. So the two long ās in the middle of the word are seams, and the word means seated on a seat made of five corpses, with each element visible once you know where to cut.

Brahma is the word reciters most often pad. It is bra plus hma, an h followed by an m within a single cluster, and there is no vowel between them. Many trained singers in both north and south insert one, producing something like ba-ra-ha-ma. Try instead to keep it two syllables: brah-ma, with the h audible as breath at the close of the first and the m beginning the second.

Svarūpiṇī has the initial cluster sv — a dental s directly into a v that in Sanskrit is closer to a soft w than to an English v — and then the retroflex ṇ. After a verse with no retroflexes at all, this ṇ and the one at the end of rūpiṇī are the only two in the whole of this one. They are easy to miss for exactly that reason.

Cinmayī hides the same sandhi you met in jagannāthā. The word is cit plus maya: a final unvoiced dental t before a nasal becomes the matching nasal n. So chanting cinmayī you are in fact saying cit, and the fourth name of the entire stotra, cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā, showed you the other outcome of the same final t, voiced to d before a vowel. One consonant, two fates, and both of them worth recognising while the word is in your mouth.

Vijñānaghanarūpiṇī gives you jñ, the cluster from mahārājñī in the first verse: a j and a palatal ñ, both made flat against the hard palate. Then gh, a genuinely aspirated g — the breath comes after the stop, not before it — and then the same -rūpiṇī ending as the second name of the verse, which is why the two eight-syllable names rhyme.

On what to hold while chanting: this is one of the very few verses in the hymn where the second half explains the first, and reciting it as six unrelated epithets throws that away. Carry the couch through the caesura. The gods are lying there because of what the second line says she is.

062.subtitle: Meditation, the meditator, and the thing meditated on

commentary.meaning: The first name collapses the three terms that any act of contemplation requires — the practice, the person doing it, the object it is aimed at — into a single subject, which means that the verse begins by dismantling the situation the reciter is currently in. The second lifts her out of the moral ledger altogether. Then the second line begins the longest sustained piece of philosophy in the thousand names: the passage through the states of consciousness, which will run on into the next verse and finish only when it has arrived at something that is not a state. Waking is named twice here, once as the whole visible world and once as the act of being awake, and dream is named twice too, once as an ordinary participle and once with the technical term the Upaniṣads use for the self that dreams. The doubling is the method. Each condition is given first as what it looks like from outside and then as who is having it, and both, the verse says, are her.
commentary.history:
Look at the first name as grammar before looking at it as doctrine, because the grammar is the argument. One root, √dhyai, to contemplate, takes three suffixes: dhyāna is the action noun, the activity itself; dhyātṛ is the agent noun in -tṛ, the one who does it; dhyeya is the gerundive in -ya, that which is to be done to, the target. Sanskrit generates such triads freely — jñāna, jñātṛ, jñeya for knowing; grahaṇa, grahītṛ, grāhya for grasping — and the tradition calls the resulting structure the triputī, the threefold. Every ordinary mental act has this shape, and the whole of Indian contemplative theory is organised around the question of what happens when it stops having it.

Patañjali's answer is the standard one and the stotra is using his vocabulary. Concentration is the mind tied to one place; meditation is the unbroken running of a single content in that place; and when the same practice goes on until only the object shines and the act seems to have lost its own form, that is absorption. The three together, applied at once, he calls saṃyama. The name dhyānadhyātṛdhyeyarūpā takes the endpoint of that process and makes it a description of her rather than of a practitioner's achievement. Which has a practical consequence for anyone reciting the verse: whatever is happening while you chant it is not something you are doing to her.

Dharmādharmavivarjitā is harder than it looks, and it is worth resisting the easy reading that she is above right and wrong in some libertine sense. Dharma in the ritual literature is very specific: it is the merit generated by performing prescribed acts, an invisible credit that ripens later, and adharma is the corresponding debit. The name says she has no entry in that account. Three verses before the end of this stretch the stotra will say that she is the one who hands out the fruits of merit and demerit to everyone else, and the two statements go together rather than colliding. The person who awards the result is not among those receiving it.

Then the states. The text behind this passage is the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, twelve sentences of prose, the shortest of the principal Upaniṣads and the one that has generated the most commentary in proportion to its length. It maps the syllable OM onto the self and the self onto four quarters. The first is the waking self, called viśva or vaiśvānara, whose awareness faces outward and whose objects are gross and public. The second is the dreaming self, taijasa, whose awareness faces inward and whose objects are subtle; the name means the luminous one, from tejas, brightness, because there is no external light in a dream and the scene has to be lit from within. The third is the sleeper. The fourth is not a fourth of the same kind, and the next verse of the stotra will deal with it.

That the stotra is following this scheme and not merely listing moods is clear from the pairing. Viśvarūpā can be read on its own as she whose form is the universe, and that reading is correct and is the one most translators give. But it stands immediately before jāgariṇī, the waking one, and viśva is precisely the Māṇḍūkya's name for the waking self, so the two names together say the state and the self of the state. Svapantī and taijasātmikā then do the same for dream, and in the next verse suptā and prājñātmikā will do it for deep sleep. Three conditions, each named twice, in strict order.

One formal detail is worth noticing while chanting. Svapantī is a present participle in the feminine — she who is sleeping — and the thousand names contain almost nothing else of the kind. Nearly every name in this hymn is a compound or a derived adjective; a live participle from a common verb is a jolt, and it comes at exactly the moment when the text wants to describe not a property she has but something she is in the middle of doing.
commentary.practice:
The first name is the most demanding cluster drill in this part of the stotra and there is no way to make it easy. Dhyānadhyātṛdhyeyarūpā has dhy three times in its first six syllables. The cluster is an aspirated dental d — tongue-tip at the back of the upper teeth, then a distinct puff of breath — followed immediately by the palatal glide y. English wants to turn the whole thing into a j. Take it apart: say a clean d, then breathe out, then y, then the vowel. Then compress it until it is one release. Then do it three times in a row.

Between the second and third occurrences sits dhyātṛ, which ends in the syllabic ṛ. It is short. It is one beat, not two, and northern reciters who render it as "ri" and southern reciters who render it as "ru" both go wrong only if they lengthen it. Whatever colour you give the vowel, keep it brief, or the eight-syllable name becomes nine.

Dharmādharma is the same seam you met in carācara two verses ago: dharma plus adharma, a short a meeting a short a and producing one long ā. The long vowel in the middle of the word is the negative particle. Shorten it and the name says the opposite of what it means. This fusion is so common in the hymn that it is worth adopting a rule of thumb — when a long ā appears in the middle of a compound with no obvious reason, suspect a hidden a-.

The second line is much gentler and is a good place to recover. Viśvarūpā opens with the palatal ś, tongue-body flat against the hard palate, followed by v, which in Sanskrit is closer to a soft w than to an English v: say śwa rather than shva. Jāgariṇī ends in a retroflex ṇ and is otherwise plain. Svapantī has the initial cluster sv and then a dental n before a dental t, which is one tongue position for both. Taijasātmikā gives you the diphthong ai, a full long vowel, and then the cluster tm, a dental into a labial, which most people manage without thinking about it.

Count the second line as four, four, three, five. Svapantī at three syllables is the shortest name in the verse and the easiest to stretch; keep it tight and the line balances.

A point of grammar that changes the sense. Jāgariṇī and taijasātmikā are both nouns describing a standing condition; svapantī, between them, is a live participle. Give it a slightly lighter, more mobile delivery than its neighbours, because it is the only word in the verse that is happening rather than being. In archanā the difference surfaces at once: viśvarūpāyai, jāgariṇyai, svapantyai, taijasātmikāyai, three dative patterns in one line.

What to hold while chanting: the first name has already told you that the meditation, the meditator and the object are the same. Everything after it in this verse and the next is an unpacking of that one claim across the whole of your day and night.

063.subtitle: The fourth, and then the first of the five acts

commentary.meaning: Eight names, and the verse is a hinge. Its first line finishes what the previous verse began: deep sleep, then the self that is present in deep sleep, then the fourth — and then, immediately, the withdrawal of even that as a description, because counting her as fourth in a series is still a way of putting her in the series. Its second line starts something entirely new. The five acts by which a world is run are introduced two at a time, each act paired with the god who performs it: the making, and Brahmā; the guarding, and Govinda. What makes the verse strange to read straight through is that these two halves are not reconciled. Four names have just said that no condition whatever can be laid over her, and the fifth name says she makes the universe. The stotra does not soften the join, and the tradition regards the absence of a join as the whole content of the verse.
commentary.history:
The Māṇḍūkya's description of dreamless sleep is one of the most quoted sentences in Indian philosophy, and it is the direct source of prājñātmikā. The sleeper wants nothing and sees nothing; awareness has become one, undivided; it is a solid mass of knowing, made of bliss, feeding on bliss. The name of that self is Prājña, from prajñā, and it means the wise one — wise not because it knows a great deal but because nothing in it is separated out to be known. The previous verse of the stotra called her a solid mass of knowing using very nearly the Upaniṣad's own compound, and here, one line later, the same idea is attached to sleep. That is not an accident of the poem. Deep sleep is the tradition's standing evidence that awareness can exist without an object.

What happens next is the subtle part, and it explains why the verse needs two names for the fourth rather than one. When the Māṇḍūkya comes to the fourth quarter, it defines it by negation, and among the things it denies is the very phrase it had just used of deep sleep: the fourth is not aware inwardly, not aware outwardly, not aware both ways, not a solid mass of knowing, not aware, not unaware. So the fourth is not sleep intensified, and it is not a better grade of the same substance. It is not on the scale. Turyā names it and sarvāvasthāvivarjitā immediately takes the name back, and Gauḍapāda's commentary makes exactly this move: the fourth is called a quarter only for the purpose of teaching, since it is not a part of anything.

One small philological point. The word appears in Sanskrit both as turya and as turīya, and the two are the same ordinal, fourth. Turya is the shorter and older-looking form; turīya, with the extra syllable, is commoner in the Upaniṣadic prose. The stotra uses turyā because it has two syllables to spend and not three.

With sṛṣṭikartrī the text changes subject and does not signal it. The five acts are creation, preservation, withdrawal, concealment and grace, and they are the standard Śaiva analysis of what divine agency consists of. The stotra will complete the list in the next verse; here it gives the first two, and it gives each of them twice, once as the act and once as the god. Brahmā is the face of making, Govinda the face of keeping. The point of doubling is the same as in the previous verse's treatment of waking and dream: to prevent the reader from settling on either the function or the personality as the real answer.

Goptrī and govinda are placed side by side and they have nothing to do with each other, which is precisely why they are placed side by side. Goptrī is an agent noun from √gup, to guard. Govinda is built on go, which means both a cow and, in older usage, the earth, and the tradition offers competing derivations to match: the finder of cows, the cowherd, or the one who recovered the earth. The names sound as though they share a root and do not, and Sanskrit poetics has a name for that kind of collision and considers it a merit rather than a coincidence.

There is one more thing worth noticing about this verse and the next, and it is structural. The five gods who are about to be listed as the agents of the five acts — Brahmā, Govinda, Rudra, Īśvarī and Sadāśiva — are the same five who two verses ago were lying under her as corpses. The stotra has shown you the five inert and is now showing you the five at work, and the only thing that has changed between the two pictures is that she has been described in the meantime as consciousness itself.
commentary.practice:
This verse is front-loaded with difficulty and then relaxes, which is unusual and worth exploiting: take the first line slowly and let the second carry you.

Suptā is a past passive participle of √svap and is only two syllables, so it goes past quickly; make sure the pt is heard as two consonants, not as a single stop. Prājñātmikā then gives you the cluster jñ, which is a j followed by the palatal nasal ñ, both made with the tongue-body flat against the hard palate. You met it in mahārājñī in the very first verse of the stotra. Northern reciters commonly say something like "gy" and southern reciters something like "jñ"; the value the grammarians describe is the second, and it is worth producing at least once deliberately even if you then revert to the pronunciation of your tradition.

Turyā has the cluster ry, an r immediately followed by y with no vowel between. The Sanskrit r is a tap of the tongue-tip, not the English glide, so tur-yā should have a flick in the middle of it.

Sarvāvasthāvivarjitā is eight syllables and looks worse than it is. The seam is sarva plus avasthā, another short a meeting a short a and giving a long ā — the same fusion as in carācara and dharmādharma. Then vi-varjitā, from vi-√vṛj, to exclude, the same word that ended the second name of the previous verse. Two names in adjacent verses ending in vivarjitā is the poet's way of bracketing the whole passage on the states, and hearing the echo tells you the passage is over.

The second line is the easier one and it contains a small paradigm lesson. Sṛṣṭikartrī and goptrī are both feminine agent nouns in -trī, from √kṛ and √gup, and they are the feminine counterparts of the -tṛ nouns like dhyātṛ in the previous verse. Sṛṣṭi opens with the syllabic ṛ followed by the retroflex pair ṣṭ, so the tongue-tip goes back and stays back for three sounds running; kartrī then piles r, t and r into one cluster. Goptrī has ptr, three consonants, and reciters routinely reduce it to "potri". Give the p its own closure.

Brahmarūpā has the same hm that you drilled in the previous verse's pañcabrahmasvarūpiṇī: an h and an m inside a single cluster, no vowel between them. Govindarūpiṇī is the only name in the verse with nothing difficult in it at all, and it is the last, which is a kindness.

The caesura is after the eighth syllable of each line: after prājñātmikā in the first, after brahmarūpā in the second. Note that the first of these falls in the middle of the passage on the states and the second in the middle of the list of acts, so in both cases you are breathing inside a thought. Let the pause be metrical rather than semantic.

What to hold while chanting: the verse asks you to say, within four seconds of each other, that no condition can be attributed to her and that she makes the world. Do not try to resolve it while chanting. The resolution, if there is one, is that making a world is not a condition.

064.subtitle: The five acts, and the last of them is grace

commentary.meaning: Seven names finish what the previous verse began, and they finish it with the two acts that make this scheme a theology rather than a cosmology. Withdrawal comes first, wearing the form of Rudra, whose name means the howler and whose terror is nothing but the act of gathering the world back in. Then concealment, and for that act she is called simply the ruler, because hiding one's own nature so that a world of separate beings can stand is an exercise of power and not a lapse in it. Then grace, twice over: once as Sadāśiva, the one whose kindness never lapses, and once as the plain statement that she is the giver of favour. The verse closes by insisting that these are not five occupations but one — parāyaṇa, her sole business, the thing she is wholly given over to.
commentary.history:
Everyone knows three of the five. Making, keeping and unmaking are common property across Indian religion, and any tradition can assign them to a trio of gods. The distinctive contribution of the Śaiva systems, and the reason this verse matters, is the addition of two more.

Tirodhāna is concealment, and the word is built out of tiras, across or aside, and √dhā, to place: to put something across, to draw a curtain over. What is concealed is her own nature. The doctrine is that a world containing separate beings who take themselves to be separate cannot exist unless the underlying identity is hidden, and that the hiding is therefore not a failure of the system but a positive act performed deliberately, the fourth thing she does. This is why the name for the agent of that act is Īśvarī, the ruler: it takes power to keep the truth about a thing out of that thing's view. Set beside dharmādharmavivarjitā two verses back, the name is quietly unsettling. The condition that makes moral life possible is one she installs.

Anugraha is the release of that curtain, and the word is anu plus √grah, a reaching after or taking hold of, used in ordinary Sanskrit for the favour a superior shows a dependent. The tradition is firm that it cannot be earned, since anything that could be earned would fall under merit, and merit has already been ruled out as a way of reaching her. That is why the stotra gives grace two names in a row: sadāśivā, where it is an unfailing disposition, and anugrahadā, where it is an act of giving. The verse takes care not to let grace be described as a payment.

The two acts are the same act in opposite directions, and the clearest statement of that anywhere is in the seventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gītā, where the veil is described as divine, as belonging to the speaker, and as impossible to cross — and then, in the second half of the same verse, as crossed by anyone who comes to him. The veiling and the unveiling are attributed to the same agent in the same breath, which is exactly the arrangement of the second line here.

The five acts also have a visual form, and if you have ever looked at a bronze Naṭarāja you have already been reading them. The drum in the upper right hand is emission. The open palm raised in reassurance is maintenance. The flame in the upper left is withdrawal. The foot planted on the crouching figure is concealment. The lifted foot is grace. The image is thus not a dance in general but this specific list, and Śaiva teachers have used it as a teaching diagram for a very long time. That the stotra placed the witness of that dance seven verses earlier and the list of what the dance does here is unlikely to be accidental.

One word in the last name repays looking up. Parāyaṇa is para, highest or furthest, plus ayana, a going: literally the furthest going, and by usage a final resort, a refuge, and then the thing a person is entirely taken up with. Pañcakṛtyaparāyaṇā therefore does not say she performs five duties. It says the five are what she is occupied with to the exclusion of everything else — which, given that the five between them account for the entire career of a universe, is a way of saying she has no private life.
commentary.practice:
Saṃhāriṇī opens the verse with an anusvāra, and this is a good place to think about what that mark actually is. The word is sam plus √hṛ, to draw together; the m of the prefix, standing before h, is written as the dot and pronounced as a nasal coloured by what follows, which here means a nasal resonance running into the h rather than a closed m. Do not shut the lips. Then the retroflex ṇ at the end, which is there because of the r earlier in the word — a rule that also gives you the ṇ in rūpiṇī, kartrī's neighbours, and half the names in this hymn.

The third name in the first line contains the single most useful sandhi in this verse, and reciters who do not know it lose a name. Tirodhānakarī ends in a long ī. Īśvarī begins with a long ī. Two long ī sounds fuse into one, so what is printed and chanted is tirodhānakarīśvarī, a single unbroken word — but there are two names inside it, and the nāmāvalī separates them: tirodhānakaryai namaḥ, then īśvaryai namaḥ. If you have only ever chanted the stotra you may never have noticed that this is two names. Listen for the long ī in the middle and know that it is a seam.

The second line opens with the other kind of seam and this one is visible on the page. Sadāśivā ends in long ā and anugrahadā begins with short a; the short a is swallowed, and Devanagari marks its disappearance with the avagraha, the small hook printed as ऽ. So सदाशिवाऽनुग्रहदा is two names, sadāśivā and anugrahadā, and the hook is telling you that an a has been elided there. Wherever you meet that mark in this text, an initial a has gone missing.

Dhāna in tirodhāna is an aspirated dental — d, then breath, then the vowel — and never the sound of English "th". Rudrarūpā has the cluster dr and then a long ū. Pañcakṛtyaparāyaṇā gives you three things at once: the palatal nasal ñ before c, the syllabic ṛ in kṛ, and the cluster ty; and it ends with the retroflex ṇ, again triggered by the r earlier in the word.

Both lines are a clean eight and eight, with the caesura falling after rudrarūpā and after anugrahadā. That means the caesura in the second line falls between the fifth act and its summary, which is a natural place to breathe and also the right place: everything before it is the list, everything after it is the comment on the list.

What to hold while chanting. There is a temptation to hear the five acts as a job description and to chant them briskly. The verse resists that in its last word. Parāyaṇa is not what somebody does; it is what somebody is entirely taken up with. And the order is not neutral: withdrawal, then concealment, then grace. The list ends where you are, which is to say inside the fourth act, waiting on the fifth.

065.subtitle: In the middle of the sun's disc

commentary.meaning: Six names in an alternating pattern of sounds — three beginning in bh, then p, bh, p — and an alternating pattern of temperaments to match. She stands at the centre of the sun, which answers the name six verses ago that placed her at the centre of the moon. Then, without preparation, Bhairavī, the terrible one. Then a garland made of the six excellences that entitle anyone to be called a lord. Then three names that all belong, in ordinary usage, to Lakṣmī and her household: seated on a lotus, the blessed one, and sister of the god with the lotus at his navel. What the verse does, quietly and without argument, is take a whole Vaiṣṇava vocabulary and settle it on her — not by conquest but by kinship. Viṣṇu ends the verse as her brother, born of the same womb, which puts the two of them on the same side of a question the sects have spent centuries arguing about.
commentary.history:
Take the first name against its counterpart. Six verses back she was candramaṇḍalamadhyagā, going in the middle of the moon's disc; here she is bhānumaṇḍalamadhyasthā, standing in the middle of the sun's. The verbs differ — √gam and √sthā — and so does the temperature. In the ritual of this school the sun, the moon and fire are three distinct luminaries, each with its own set of digits, and each is worshipped into a different vessel before the main rite begins: fire into the base, the sun into the offering vessel, the moon into the water. So the pairing of these two names is not a poetic symmetry. It is a report of a liturgical fact, and a third name for the fire is not needed because she has already been described as born from one.

The person in the sun is the oldest continuously maintained object of contemplation in the tradition, and this name is claiming his seat. The Chāndogya describes him with a golden beard and golden hair and gold to the very tips of his nails; the Īśa asks the sun to withdraw its blaze so the face inside it can be seen; and the Gāyatrī, which is still recited at dawn, noon and dusk by anyone keeping the old discipline, meditates on the light of the sun-god and nothing else. To be at the centre of the solar orb is to be what all of that has been aimed at.

Bhairavī, dropped between the sun and the garland with no transition at all, is the feminine of Bhairava, who was named eight verses ago as her worshipper. She is also a goddess in her own right — Tripurabhairavī, one of the ten Mahāvidyās — and the stotra is content to give her the fierce name in the middle of a line otherwise full of light and flowers. That kind of placement is characteristic of this text: it does not build up to its fierce names and does not apologise afterwards.

Bhaga is a rich word and worth ten minutes with a dictionary. Its root is √bhaj, to divide, to apportion, to allot; from that come a share, a portion, and then good fortune, prosperity, dignity, majesty, excellence, loveliness. Bhaga is also the name of a Vedic Āditya, the apportioner who distributes shares. And the classic definition, quoted everywhere in the theistic literature, fixes the sense at six: total sovereignty, power, fame, beauty, knowledge and non-attachment. Bhagamālinī says those six hang on her in a wreath; bhagavatī, four names later, says she possesses them. The same word twice, once as an ornament and once as a title. Bhagamālinī is also the name of the second of the fifteen Nityā goddesses worshipped in the Śrīcakra, so the name has a second address in the ritual as well as a meaning in the dictionary.

The last name is the most interesting and the most easily skated over. Sahodara does not mean brother in a loose or honorary sense. It is saha, together, plus udara, the belly: born from one womb. So the stotra is not saying that Viṣṇu behaves towards her as a brother would; it is asserting a shared origin. There are two strands behind the claim. In the purāṇic account of her marriage to Śiva, Viṣṇu performs the office of the bride's brother and gives her away — a role still enacted every year in the great wedding festival at Madurai, where Viṣṇu arrives to hand Mīnākṣī to Sundareśvara and the whole city turns out for it. And in the Devī Māhātmya the power that sleeps in Viṣṇu at the end of a world-age is the goddess herself, so the relation is prior to either of them having a story. Padmanābha, lotus-navelled, is the epithet that carries the cosmogony: the lotus grows from his navel and Brahmā sits on it. Calling her his uterine sister places her one step behind the point where that lotus opens.
commentary.practice:
The verse is built on the aspirated labial bh, and there is one thing to fix before anything else. Bh is a single consonant, not b followed by h. The lips close for a b, and the breath comes out after the release, voiced. Say a normal b, then add the breath to the release without inserting a vowel: bhā, not b'hā and not bə-hā. You get four goes at it in this verse — bhānu, bhairavī, bhaga, bhagavatī — and one more inside padmanābha, where it sits between two vowels and is even easier to soften into a plain b.

Bhairavī has the diphthong ai, which is a full-length vowel in Sanskrit, roughly as long as ā. Reciters who treat it as a short glide will clip the name to two beats and lose a syllable from the line.

Bhānumaṇḍalamadhyasthā is the longest word in the verse and it packs three separate difficulties into its second half. Maṇḍala has the retroflex pair ṇḍ, tongue-tip curled back for both. Madhya has dhy, an aspirated dental with the palatal glide. Sthā has sth, a dental s straight into an aspirated dental t — three consonants in a row from three different sources with no vowel to help. Take the word as bhānu, maṇḍala, madhya, sthā, and rebuild it slowly.

It is worth setting this name beside candramaṇḍalamadhyagā from the fifty-ninth verse and saying the two one after the other. They share ten syllables and diverge only at the end, and the divergence is a real difference in meaning: -sthā is from √sthā, to stand, and -gā is from √gam, to go. She stands in the sun and moves in the moon.

The second line is much softer. Padmāsanā is padma plus āsana, with the usual short a plus long ā giving one long ā at the seam; the cluster dm, a dental into a labial, is the same one you have met in padmarāga. Bhagavatī has no clusters at all and three short a sounds in a row, which is the trap — under speed the three tend to lengthen unevenly. Keep them all short and equal: bha-ga-va-tī.

Padmanābhasahodarī divides as padma, nābha, saha, udara, with the a of saha and the u of udara fusing to give o. That is the same guṇa fusion as in the next verse's nimiṣotpanna, and knowing it is what lets you hear the word udara, belly, inside a name that otherwise looks opaque.

Count the lines as eight, three, five and then four, four, eight. Bhairavī at three syllables is the shortest name here and, like all the short names in this hymn, the one most likely to be stretched. Give it exactly three beats and move on.

What to hold while chanting: the verse begins in the hottest place there is and ends in a family. If it is used as a contemplation on its own, the thing to sit with is the first name — not the sun, but the middle of it, which is a place nobody can look at.
