066.subtitle: Rows of worlds, made and unmade in a blink

commentary.meaning: Two lines that come from opposite ends of the tradition and are set side by side without comment. The first is one name sixteen syllables long, and it says that the ranks of worlds come into being when she opens her eyes and go out of being when she shuts them — an image of cosmic time as a nervous tic, and one that belongs to the vocabulary of the schools that treat consciousness as a pulse. The second line is the opening of the Puruṣa Sūkta, the hymn of the cosmic person from the tenth book of the Ṛgveda, quoted almost word for word with the gender changed: a thousand heads and faces, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. So the verse puts the oldest cosmology in the language next to one of the latest, and the seam between them is the eye. The Vedic person has a thousand of them; the name before says what happens each time they close.
commentary.history:
Unmeṣa and nimeṣa are the opening and the shutting of the eyelids, and nimeṣa is also the standard Sanskrit unit for the shortest measurable stretch of time — the blink is what you divide time by. So the first name is not merely saying that worlds appear and vanish at her pleasure. It is saying they appear and vanish within the smallest interval anyone can name, which is a very different claim: not that she destroys the world but that the world's arising and perishing are continuous and are happening now.

That pair of words is the signature of a particular school. The foundational verse of the Spanda tradition of Kashmir — spanda means a throb, a vibration, the smallest possible movement — opens by praising Śaṅkara as the one by whose unmeṣa and nimeṣa the world dissolves and appears. The Spanda literature grows out of the Śiva Sūtras associated with Vasugupta and is usually placed in the ninth century, and its whole project is to describe reality as a pulsation rather than a substance. Whether the sahasranāma is drawing on that literature, or the two are drawing on a formula older than either, cannot be settled: the date of this stotra is not established, and the estimates that scholars offer are wide. What can be said is that the vocabulary is identical and that the idea does not appear in this form in the older strata of the tradition.

Āvalī, the last element of the compound, means a row, a line, a series. She does not make and unmake a world; she makes and unmakes rows of them. The purāṇas are comfortable with an unbounded plurality of world-eggs, and the third verse of this very stotra had them floating submerged in her red radiance. Utpanna and vipanna are two past participles of the same root, √pad, with different prefixes — arisen and gone to ruin — and they rhyme on purpose. The whole life of a world is the difference between two syllables.

Then the register changes completely. The Puruṣa Sūkta is one of the latest hymns in the Ṛgveda and by far the most influential; it describes a cosmic person with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes and a thousand feet, who is sacrificed and out of whose body the world and its orders are made. Its first line is what the stotra's second line is. The changes are small and worth counting: sahasraśīrṣā, thousand-headed, becomes sahasraśīrṣavadanā, with faces added; sahasrākṣaḥ becomes sahasrākṣī, the feminine; and sahasrapāt is left exactly as the Veda has it. That last is a small grammatical event. Nearly every one of the thousand names is a feminine nominative singular in long ā or long ī. This one ends in a consonant, because pād- is an old root noun and the stotra has chosen not to smooth it into a regular feminine. For one word the hymn is speaking Vedic.

Sahasra means a thousand and, like the same figure in most languages, also means uncountably many. It is not a coincidence that it appears three times in a hymn of a thousand names. The Ṛgvedic hymn used the number to say that the cosmic person exceeds enumeration; the stotra has organised itself around the same number and is here quoting the source of the convention.

The Bhagavad Gītā's eleventh chapter does the same thing at greater length and is the middle term between the two. Arjuna sees a form with numberless arms, bellies, mouths and eyes, and no beginning, middle or end that he can find. The vocabulary is the Puruṣa Sūkta's and the situation is a vision rather than a hymn, which is the step this stotra also takes: the Vedic hymn describes a person, and the later texts describe someone looking at one.
commentary.practice:
The first line is a single word of sixteen syllables, and there is no way to chant it except as one arc. Its pieces are unmeṣa, nimiṣa, utpanna, vipanna, bhuvanāvalī. Fix them by their sense: eyes open, eyes shut, arisen, perished, rows of worlds. Once you can say those five in English you can say the name.

The join between the second and third pieces is the most instructive sandhi in this stretch of the stotra. Nimiṣa ends in a short a; utpanna begins with a short u; a plus u gives o. So nimiṣotpanna is nimiṣa plus utpanna, and the o in the middle is a fusion, not a vowel that belongs to either word. You have already met the companion rule in maheśvara, where a plus i gave e. Between them, e and o account for most of the vowels in this text that seem to come from nowhere.

Unmeṣa and nimiṣa both end in a retroflex ṣ. Note that the stotra writes nimiṣa where the Kashmiri verse writes nimeṣa: both are formed from √miṣ, to open the eyes, and the difference is only the vowel grade, so neither is a mistake. Whichever you say, keep the ṣ retroflex — tongue-tip curled back — and distinguish it from the palatal ś you will meet in the next line's śīrṣa.

Utpanna and vipanna each have a doubled n, and the doubling has to be heard: ut-pan-na, not utpana. The metre depends on the length the doubled consonant gives the preceding syllable.

The second line is a drill in three sounds that occur close together. Sahasra has the cluster sr, dental s into r. Śīrṣa has the palatal ś at the front and the retroflex ṣ after an r — so the tongue starts flat against the hard palate and ends curled back, in one syllable. Sahasrākṣī has kṣ, which Sanskrit treats as a single conjunct: a k released directly into a retroflex ṣ. Run sahasraśīrṣa and sahasrākṣī against each other slowly and you will have covered two of the three sibilants and the retroflex series in about four seconds.

Sahasrapāt is the one name in this part of the hymn that does not end in a vowel. The stem is pād-, foot, and at the end of a word a voiced d is devoiced to t, which is why the citation form is pāt. In archanā this produces an unusual dative too — sahasrapade namaḥ — because a consonant stem does not take the -āyai of the ā-stems. Doing that one deliberately is worth more than reading a page of a grammar.

The caesura in the second line falls after sahasraśīrṣavadanā, so the line breathes eight and then four plus four. In the first line there is no caesura you can use, only a metrical one inside vi-panna. Take a full breath before beginning and do not plan to take another.

What to hold while chanting: the first name is describing something happening at this moment and at the rate of a blink, not an event at the end of time. If the verse is used as a contemplation, that is where to stay.

067.subtitle: Mother from Brahmā down to the worm

commentary.meaning: Four names, each of them eight syllables, and between them they cover the four things any traditional account of the world has to explain: where living beings come from, how society is arranged, where scripture gets its authority, and why actions have consequences. Nothing here describes her. Every name states a relation between her and everything else. She is mother of the whole range of living things, and the range is given as a span with its two ends named — the creator god at the top and an insect at the bottom, with no suggestion that her motherhood is graded along it. The divisions of class and the stages of a life are her arrangement. Revealed scripture carries authority because it is her own order put into words. And the results of good and bad action are not self-generating; they are handed out, and she is the one who hands them out.
commentary.history:
Ābrahmakīṭa is a span, not a list. The prefix ā, used with what is grammatically an ablative sense, means as far as, extending up to; the idiom is common in Sanskrit and turns up in phrases like ābrahmastambaparyanta, from Brahmā as far as a clump of grass, which is the standard way of saying every living thing without exception. Putting the two extremes in one compound and then calling herself the mother of the whole interval is a stronger statement than a general claim of universal motherhood would be, because it forces the reader to picture both ends at once.

Varṇāśrama is a single compound covering the two axes along which classical Indian society was described: the four varṇas, and the four āśramas or stages of a life — student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer. The dharmaśāstra literature treats the pair as exhaustive, so varṇāśramadharma is simply the whole of normative social life. What the name adds is vidhāyinī, from vi-√dhā, to arrange, ordain, lay down. She is not said to sanction the arrangement; she is said to have made it. The Bhagavad Gītā's formulation of the same claim is more careful, and the care is worth noticing: the four classes were created by me according to the distribution of quality and action — and know me also to be the one who does not act. The stotra offers no such qualification here, which is a fact about the text worth registering rather than smoothing over, particularly since five verses earlier it declared her free of merit and demerit altogether.

Nigama, in the third name, is one of the standard words for revealed scripture, and it is normally used of the Vedic corpus specifically, in contrast with āgama, which is used of the tantric. The two words are a matched pair and the next verse of the stotra will use the other one. So over two verses the hymn claims both bodies of revelation, and it does so in different figures: here the Veda is her command, there the whole mass of tantric scripture is an oyster shell with her inside it.

The claim in nijājñārūpanigamā is precise and it takes a side in an old argument. Ājñā is a command, from ā-√jñā, to make known; nija means one's own. The Veda, the name says, is her command wearing the form of words. The Mīmāṃsā school, whose whole business was the interpretation of Vedic injunction, held the opposite: the Veda is apauruṣeya, not made by any person, without an author human or divine, and its authority rests precisely on the fact that no one issued it, since anyone who issued it could have been mistaken. The theistic schools took the other line and cited the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's image of the Vedas breathed out of the great being like smoke from damp fuel. This name is a two-word summary of that position.

The fourth name takes a side in the neighbouring argument. If a sacrifice performed today produces a result years later, what carries the result across the interval? Mīmāṃsā answered with apūrva, an unseen potency generated by the act itself and ripening on its own, and pointedly did not require a god. Vedānta answered that the fruit comes from the Lord, and the Brahma Sūtra makes the case in three words — phalam ata upapatteḥ, the fruit is from him, because that is what makes sense — arguing that an inert potency cannot apportion rewards. Puṇyāpuṇyaphalapradā puts her in that role. The interest of the name lies in what it does to the preceding one. If she both issues the injunctions and delivers the results of obeying or disobeying them, then the moral order is not a mechanism she supervises. It is an arrangement, made and administered by the same person, and the last thing the stotra said about her own standing in it is that she is not in it.
commentary.practice:
This is the most metrically regular verse in the whole stretch: four names, four quarters, eight syllables each, one name filling each quarter exactly. Nothing straddles a boundary, and the caesura in each line falls cleanly between two names. After the sixteen-syllable monsters of the last verse and the one before, it is a chance to feel the anuṣṭubh's basic shape with nothing complicating it.

Ābrahmakīṭajananī begins with a long ā that is doing grammatical work: it is the prefix meaning as far as, and it is the whole reason the name means from Brahmā rather than of Brahmā. Shortening it does not just mispronounce the word, it removes the preposition. Then brahma gives you hm inside a single cluster once again — h and m with no vowel between, the same problem as in pañcabrahmasvarūpiṇī and brahmarūpā — and kīṭa gives you a retroflex ṭ after a long ī. Jananī, three plain dental n sounds after that retroflex, is a good contrast: tongue-tip back for kīṭa, then forward for all of jananī.

Varṇāśramavidhāyinī has the retroflex ṇ in varṇa, triggered by the r before it, and then the palatal ś in āśrama, and then dhy in vidhāyinī. The seam is varṇa plus āśrama, a short a meeting a long ā to give one long ā, which is the same fusion as in padmāsanā in the previous verse and in carācara before that. It has now appeared often enough to be treated as a habit rather than a rule.

Nijājñārūpanigamā contains the cluster jñ immediately after a long ā, which is awkward because the tongue has to come up to the hard palate from an open vowel with no transition. Say ni-jā-jñā slowly. The last element, nigama, is all short vowels and is easy to rush past, which is a pity, since it is the word that tells you what the name is about.

Puṇyāpuṇyaphalapradā is the neatest word in the verse and the most satisfying to say. It is puṇya plus apuṇya — merit and its negation, with the negating a swallowed into the long ā at the seam, exactly as in dharmādharma five verses earlier — then phala, fruit, then pradā, giver. Both occurrences of puṇya have the retroflex ṇ followed by y, which is a genuinely difficult sequence: the tongue-tip is curled back for the ṇ and then has to spring forward and flat for the y. Do not let the ṇ soften into a dental n on the second occurrence, which is where the fatigue shows.

In archanā all four names take the ordinary -āyai of the feminine ā-stems, so this verse is also the simplest one in the neighbourhood to practise that ending on: ābrahmakīṭajananyai namaḥ is the only irregular one, because jananī is an ī-stem and takes -yai.

What to hold while chanting: the verse is a set of four claims about jurisdiction and it reads coldly if you take it as an inventory. The warmth is in the first name and the first name governs the rest. The same person who laid down the social order and dispenses the results of everything anyone does is being described, in the same breath, as the mother of an insect.

068.subtitle: Vermilion in the parting of the Vedas

commentary.meaning: Two names, one to a line, each sixteen syllables, and each a single sustained image. This is the most purely literary verse in this part of the stotra: it stops arguing and makes pictures. In the first, the Vedas are prostrate at her feet, and they are so low that the dust from her lotus feet has settled along the parting of their hair — and because the dust is red, what it has made there is the vermilion streak that a married woman wears. Scripture is not merely bowing; it is being given the mark of good fortune by the act of bowing. In the second, the entire mass of revealed texts is an oyster, its two shells closed, and she is the single pearl inside. The first image makes scripture a devotee, the second makes it a container, and both agree on the thing the previous verse had already asserted in flatter language: the texts do not have authority in their own right. They have her.
commentary.history:
Śruti means what has been heard, from √śru, and it is the technical term for the Vedic revelation as distinct from smṛti, what has been remembered, which covers the secondary literature. The same word also means the ear itself, and in music a microtone. All three senses are alive in the compound, which is one reason the image works: a parting of the hair is a line running back between two ears.

Sīmanta is that parting, and it is not a neutral word. There is a rite of the same name in the household ritual, the sīmantonnayana, the drawing up of the parting, performed for a woman in pregnancy; so the term arrives already carrying marriage and motherhood. Sindūra is vermilion, and the mark of it worn in the parting is, across much of India, the visible sign that a woman's husband is alive. Put the two together and the compound says something more precise than that the Vedas are humbled. It says they have been made auspicious.

The grammar of the middle element is worth a moment because it is a construction learners rarely meet. Sindūrīkṛta is built with what the grammarians call the cvi formation: a noun whose final vowel is lengthened to ī and which is then joined to a form of √kṛ, to make, or √bhū, to become. It means made into something it was not before. So the dust has not merely landed on the parting; it has been turned into vermilion by landing there. Once you can recognise the -ī-kṛta and -ī-bhūta pattern you will find it everywhere in this literature, and it always carries that sense of conversion.

Why her foot-dust should be red is a question the stotra answered long before this verse. Everything about her is red — the meditation verses insisted on it three times over, and the third verse of the hymn had her radiance rising until the world-eggs floated in it. Red is the colour of will in this tradition, the first stirring by which anything comes to be. The dust is red because she is.

The image also has a specific target. The Upaniṣads are conventionally called the head of the Veda — vedānta, the end of it, and śrutiśiras, the crown — and the Saundaryalaharī builds a whole verse out of the fact, saying the heads of the Vedas carry her feet as a crest ornament. The sahasranāma's compound lands the dust precisely there. The most exalted part of the most authoritative text is where the mark goes.

The second line changes figure and keeps the argument. Āgama, revealed scripture, is the tantric counterpart of nigama, the word the previous verse used for the Vedic corpus; over two consecutive verses the hymn has claimed both bodies of revelation. Sandoha means a mass or aggregate, and its etymology is charming — sam plus √duh, to milk, so a sandoha is everything that has been milked together into one vessel. Śukti is the pearl-oyster. Sampuṭa is a casket made of two hemispherical halves that close on each other, and the word also has a ritual life of its own in mantra practice, where to sampuṭa a mantra is to enclose it between repetitions of another one, exactly as a pearl is enclosed. Mauktika is the pearl.

There is a classical belief behind the picture. Sanskrit poets held that pearls form when raindrops fall into an open oyster during a particular asterism, and the image recurs constantly in court poetry: something small and ordinary falls from above into something that then closes over it and turns it into a jewel. Applied here, the figure says that the whole of revelation, milked together into one shell, has exactly one thing in it, and that the shell is shut. Which is why the Upaniṣads themselves warn that the pearl does not come out for study alone.
commentary.practice:
Two names, one filling each line, and both of them ending in -ikā. The rhyme is exact and it is not an accident of the language; consecutive lines rhyming this cleanly are rare in the hymn, and hearing dhūlikā answer mauktikā is what tells you the two images are one statement.

The caesura in each line falls after the eighth syllable, and in both cases it falls inside the name. In the first line that puts it after sindūrī, which means the pause comes between the vermilion and the making of it. In the second it falls after sandoha, between the mass of scripture and the shell — which is the seam of the metaphor, so this is one place where the metrical pause and the sense agree. Hear the break without opening a gap in the sound.

Śruti opens with śr, a palatal ś directly into r. The ś is made with the tongue-body flat against the hard palate, and the r is a single tap of the tongue-tip, so the two use different parts of the tongue and can be produced together if you stop trying to sequence them. Then sīmanta gives you a dental s, a long ī and a dental n before a dental t, which is a whole quarter of the line with the tongue-tip forward.

Sindūrī has the long ī of the cvi suffix and it must be long; that vowel is the grammar. Kṛta then gives you the syllabic ṛ, short, one beat. Pādābja is pāda plus abja, with two short a sounds fusing into the long ā at the seam, and abja itself is worth knowing: ap, water, plus ja, born — the water-born, one of the many Sanskrit words for a lotus. The cluster bj, a labial into a palatal, is the hardest thing in the line and reciters routinely soften it to bija. Give the b its own closure and release.

Dhūlikā ends the line with an aspirated dh: d at the teeth, then breath, then the vowel. Never the English th.

The second line is easier but has three retroflexes hiding in it. Śukti has ś then a plain kt. Sampuṭa has a retroflex ṭ, and the anusvāra before the p is realised as a labial m, since an anusvāra always takes the place of articulation of whatever follows it. Mauktika opens with the diphthong au, which is a full-length vowel, and then kt again.

One long chain of long vowels runs through the first line — sī, dū, rī, pā, dāb, dhū — and almost none through the second, which is nearly all short until mauktikā. The two lines therefore feel completely different in weight even though they have the same number of syllables. That contrast is worth preserving rather than smoothing out: let the first line be slow and the second brisk.

In archanā both names take the ordinary -āyai, and both are long enough that the dative is a genuine feat of breath control. It is worth doing once.

What to hold while chanting: the verse is about scripture, and you are performing scripture while you say it. The first name puts the texts on the floor and the second shuts them in a shell, and neither is an insult. Both are ways of saying that what you are reciting is not the thing you are reciting it about.

069.subtitle: Fullness, and the plainest of her names

commentary.meaning: Seven names, and the verse keeps switching register. It opens technically: she grants the four recognised aims of a human life, a scheme with a name and a literature behind it. Then one flat enormous word — full. Then the enjoyer, which puts her on the subject side of the oldest distinction in Indian philosophy, the one between the experiencer and what is experienced. Then a title that is also the name of a particular goddess, sovereign of the worlds. And then, in the middle of the verse, with no compound and no ornament, ambikā: mother, the word a child uses, three syllables, the plainest name in the hymn so far. After it the verse widens out again to no beginning and no end, and closes with the three great gods in attendance. The shape is deliberate. The smallest word sits at the centre of the largest claims.
commentary.history:
The puruṣārthas are the four things a human life is understood to be for: dharma, the doing of what one ought; artha, the securing of means; kāma, pleasure and desire; and mokṣa, release. The older texts count three, the trivarga, and mokṣa is added to make the standard four. Puruṣārthapradā says she grants all of them, and the claim has already been made once in this stretch: the Saundaryalaharī verse quoted at the fifty-sixth verse of this hymn distinguished her tantra from the sixty-four precisely by saying that hers assembles every human aim at once while each of the others yields only one thing. What is a whole verse there is one word here.

Pūrṇā is the flattest word in the verse and the largest. Its classic statement is the peace invocation that stands at the head of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka: that is full, this is full, the full comes out of the full, and when you take the full away from the full, what is left over is the full. It is not a mystical paradox so much as a definition. A thing is full in this sense if no operation performed on it changes the amount, which rules out fullness being a quantity at all.

Bhoginī then places her on one side of a division that Sāṃkhya and Vedānta both organise themselves around: bhoktṛ and bhogya, the enjoyer and the enjoyed, the experiencer and the experienced. Everything that can be an object is bhogya; what has experiences is bhoktṛ. To call her the enjoyer is to say that in every experience anyone has, the one actually having it is her. There is a second sense the dictionary records and it is hard to believe a tradition this attentive to serpents left it unnoticed: bhogin also means a snake, from a different bhoga meaning the coil or the expanded hood of one.

Bhuvaneśvarī is a title — mistress of the worlds — and also the proper name of a specific goddess, one of the ten Mahāvidyās, whose seed-syllable is hrīṃ. That is worth holding on to for one more verse, because the very next verse of the stotra names hrīṃ twice. The syllable and the goddess belong together, and the hymn has just introduced them in order.

Ambikā is the one to slow down for. It is amba, mother, with the affectionate suffix -kā, and it is by a long way the least elaborate name in this part of the hymn. It is also very old and its earliest use is not what a reader of the purāṇas would expect. In the Tryambaka offering of the White Yajurveda, Rudra is given his share and told to enjoy it together with his sister Ambikā, and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, explaining the rite, says outright that Ambikā is the name of his sister. In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa she is identified with the autumn, the season of fevers, and the pair of them together are said to strike down creatures. She becomes Śiva's wife later, and by the time of the Devī Māhātmya, Ambikā is one of the principal names of the great goddess. Traditional commentators, uncomfortable with the sibling reading, gloss the Vedic word differently. Either way, the name in this verse has the longest continuous history of anything in the verse and the shortest form.

Anādinidhanā is a compound of two negatives sharing one prefix: no ādi, beginning, and no nidhana, which literally means a laying down and by usage means death or cessation. The formula is old and is applied to Brahman in the epic literature. Placed immediately after ambikā, it produces the verse's sharpest juxtaposition: the word a child uses, and then the statement that no date can be put at either end of her.

The last name lists her attendants and the list is worth reading for who is missing. Hari, Brahmā and Indra — the preserver, the creator and the king of the gods — are in attendance. Śiva is not on the list, and he is not on it because in this system he is not a servant. Twelve verses earlier the stotra called her his consecrated queen.
commentary.practice:
The first line alternates long names and short ones — six syllables, two, three, five — and the two-syllable pūrṇā in second position is the one most likely to be rushed. It carries a long ū and a retroflex ṇ and it deserves its full weight; the whole line hinges on it.

Puruṣārthapradā has the retroflex ṣ in the middle of an otherwise soft word, and the seam is puruṣa plus artha, two short a sounds fusing into a long ā. That fusion has now appeared in carācara, dharmādharma, sarvāvastha, varṇāśrama, padmāsana and puṇyāpuṇya. If a long ā turns up in the middle of a compound in this hymn and you cannot see why, look for a lost short vowel.

Pūrṇā and bhuvaneśvarī both end in retroflex sounds preceded, at some distance, by an r; that is the rule that produces most of the retroflex nasals in the text, and once you know it you can predict them rather than memorise them. Bhoginī, sitting between them, has a plain dental n, which makes the first line a three-step drill: retroflex, dental, retroflex.

Bhoginī and bhuvaneśvarī also give you the aspirated bh twice. Lips closed for a b, breath out on the release, no vowel inserted.

The second line opens with a mark that hides a name boundary, and this is the second time in six verses. Ambikā ends in a long ā; anādinidhanā begins with a short a; the short a is elided and Devanagari prints the small hook, the avagraha, in its place — अम्बिकाऽनादिनिधना. Two names, not one. The fourth verse of this group did the same thing with sadāśivā and anugrahadā. Whenever you see that hook, expect a swallowed a and a seam.

Haribrahmendrasevitā is the fourth guṇa fusion in this batch of verses and by now it should be automatic: brahma ends in short a, indra begins with short i, and a plus i gives e. So brahmendra is two gods and the e between them is the join. The name also gives you brahma with its hm cluster one last time — h and m inside a single conjunct, no vowel between them — and there is nowhere in this hymn where that word is easy.

Count the second line as eight and eight, with the caesura falling exactly between the two names. That is a rest, after a first line broken into four unequal pieces.

What to hold while chanting: everything in this verse is enormous except one word, and the enormous things are arranged around it. If the verse is used as a contemplation on its own, stop on ambikā. It is three syllables, it is the oldest name here, and it is what the whole apparatus of the preceding sixty-eight verses has been elaborating.

070.subtitle: Where the fourth digit ends and the fifth begins

commentary.meaning: Two lines, one alliterating on n and one on h, and between them this recension prints a heading, because a boundary in the structure of the whole hymn falls inside this single verse. The first line begins with a proper name borrowed from Viṣṇu, moves to undivided sound, and ends by declaring that she has no name and no form at all — which is the three hundredth of the thousand names, and closes the fourth of the divisions the text is laid out in. The second line opens the fifth, and it opens it with a syllable rather than a word: hrīṃ, twice over, then the heart, then freedom from anything to be taken up or put down. The join between the two lines is the whole point. The first ends by saying that no name will hold her; the second begins by giving her the one thing in the language that is not a name, a sound with no meaning at all, which is precisely what a seed-syllable is.
commentary.history:
Start with the structure, because this is the verse where it becomes visible. The recension this site follows divides the text into twelve sections and labels each one in the margin. The first is called the upoddhāta, the prologue. Then come ten labelled divisions of a hundred names each: tāpinī for names one to a hundred, dhūmrikā for the second hundred, marīci for the third, jvālinī for the fourth, ruci, suṣumṇā, bhogadā, viśvā, bodhinī and dhāriṇī. The twelfth and last, covering the phalaśruti, is kṣamā.

Those are not arbitrary labels. Take the ritual handbooks of this school, which have the practitioner worship the digits of fire into the base, the digits of the sun into the offering vessel and the digits of the moon into the water. The sun is given twelve digits and they are named, in order: tapinī, tāpinī, dhūmrā, marīci, jvālinī, ruci, suṣumṇā, bhogadā, viśvā, bodhinī, dhāriṇī, kṣamā. Set that list against the margins of this text and they agree from the second to the twelfth, with only the first renamed for its contents. The thousand names have been laid out on the twelve digits of the sun. Sixty-nine verses ago the hymn placed her at the centre of the lunar disc and five verses ago at the centre of the solar one; the arrangement of the text she is being praised in is, if the labels are taken at their word, the sun's own.

Whether that arrangement is original or was imposed by an editor is not something the text says, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. What can be seen is where the seam falls. Nāmarūpavivarjitā, free of name and form, is the three hundredth name and the last word of the fourth digit. Hrīṅkārī, she who utters hrīṃ, is the three hundred and first and the first word of the fifth. A hymn of a thousand names closes a hundred of them on the name that says she has none.

Nārāyaṇī is a straightforward feminine derived from Nārāyaṇa, and the traditional etymology of that name turns on the waters: nāra is taken as the waters, and ayana as a resting place, so Nārāyaṇa is the one whose resting place is the waters — the god asleep on the cosmic ocean between one world and the next. The Devī Māhātmya uses Nārāyaṇī as the refrain of its longest hymn, ending eighteen consecutive verses with the same three words, and this stotra picks up a name that had already been established as the goddess's own.

Nādarūpā requires a piece of tantric phonology. In this literature speech is described as unfolding through levels: an utterly undivided supreme speech; then paśyantī, the seeing level, where something is present but not yet articulated; then madhyamā, the middle, where it has structure but no sound; then vaikharī, the level of audible speech. Nāda is the resonance that belongs to the earliest of these, sound before it has broken into syllables and therefore before it can mean anything. To call her nādarūpā is to place her body at that level, which is why the very next name can deny her a name at all. And it is why the second line can then give her hrīṃ. A bīja is a syllable that has been deliberately kept from becoming a word.

Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī, whom the previous verse named. It is also called the māyā-bīja and the hṛllekhā, and the Saundaryalaharī's coded spelling of the fifteen-syllabled mantra ends each of its three segments with one. So hrīṅkārī is not a general statement that she makes sacred noises; it names the specific syllable that punctuates her own mantra three times.

The pun in hrīmatī is genuine and is old. Hrī is also an ordinary Sanskrit noun meaning shame, bashfulness, modesty, and in that sense Hrī is a goddess: the closing anuvāka of the Puruṣa Sūkta names Hrī and Lakṣmī as the two consorts of the Person. So the syllable and the virtue are spelt the same, and the stotra puts hrīṅkārī and hrīmatī side by side so that both readings sound at once — she who utters the seed-syllable, and she who possesses modesty.

The verse then ends on a technical pair. Heya and upādeya, what is to be rejected and what is to be taken up, are the terms in which both the yoga literature and the medical literature frame a course of treatment: identify what must go, identify what must be adopted, act accordingly. Yoga Sūtra 2.16 puts the whole of the practice under the first of them, saying that the suffering which has not yet come is what is to be avoided. Heyopādeyavarjitā says that in her case the distinction has nothing to work on, which quietly closes the door on the entire project the reciter is presumably engaged in.
commentary.practice:
The verse is two breathing exercises, one on n and one on h, and they should not sound alike.

The first line is four, four and eight, the same shape as the fifty-ninth verse. Every name begins with a dental n, and there is exactly one retroflex in the whole line: the ṇ at the end of nārāyaṇī, which is there because of the r earlier in the word. So the drill is nā-rā-ya-ṇī with the tongue-tip forward for the first n and curled back for the last, and then nādarūpā and nāmarūpavivarjitā entirely forward. If you can hear the single retroflex in a line of dentals you have solved a problem that recurs on nearly every page of this hymn.

Nāmarūpavivarjitā ends in the same vivarjitā you have already met twice in this group of verses, at sarvāvasthāvivarjitā and dharmādharmavivarjitā. Three occurrences of one word inside nine verses is unusual for this text, and the last of them is where a division of the hymn ends.

The second line is the hard one and hrīṃ is the reason. In Devanagari it is ह्रीं: an h that is a full consonant in its own right, released directly into an r, then a long ī, then the nasal. English never begins a syllable this way and the instinct is to insert a vowel and produce something like hirīṃ. Do not. Start the breath for the h, and while it is still running, tap the tongue-tip for the r. It is one movement.

In hrīṅkārī the nasal has changed shape. The syllable is hrīṃ, and when the anusvāra meets the k of kāra it takes the place of articulation of that k and becomes the guttural nasal ṅ. So the written form is hrīṅkārī and what you are saying is hrīṃ plus kāra, the standard way Sanskrit names a sound — the same construction as oṃkāra. Knowing that keeps the seed-syllable audible inside the name.

Hṛdyā is the tightest word in the verse: an h, then the syllabic ṛ, then the cluster dy. Two syllables, three difficulties. Take it as hṛd, the word for heart, plus the suffix -ya, and remember that the ṛ is short.

Heyopādeya is the last of the vowel fusions in this batch of verses: heya ends in short a, upādeya begins with short u, and a plus u gives o. That o in the middle of the word is a seam, and the word means the rejected and the accepted.

Count the second line as three, three, two and eight; hṛdyā, the shortest name in the verse, is the easiest to swallow between two long ones.

On traditional use: a division of the text ends inside this verse, and the printed editions that carry the marginal labels put the heading between the two lines. Whether you pause there or not, it is worth knowing while chanting that the hymn chose to make its break at the point where it stops using words and starts using a syllable.

What to hold while chanting: the second name says she is sound before it divides, the third says no name will fit, and the fourth gives her a syllable that means nothing. Those three are one thought, and it is the thought a reciter of a thousand names most needs and least wants.
